stem:
Priya adds baking soda to water at 20 °C in a steel tumbler at home. Some baking soda settles at the bottom and does not dissolve, even after stirring.

She then warms the mixture gently to 50 °C while stirring.

What will Priya most likely observe?

options.text: The undissolved baking soda dissolves, and more baking soda can dissolve at the higher temperature.
The baking soda at the bottom turns into a new compound when warmed.
Heating only warms the water; the amount of baking soda that can dissolve stays the same.
The undissolved baking soda floats to the top and forms a separate layer.

teacher.key_rationale: In the baking soda and water activity, raising the temperature from about 20 °C to 50 °C while stirring causes the undissolved solid to dissolve and increases the amount of baking soda the water can hold, so A is correct. Option C is the expected trap for a student who believes heating only warms the water without changing solubility; B wrongly treats warming as a chemical change; D wrongly describes a density-based separation.
